variants.name: JVM primitives: @volatile flag + join
variants.implementation_notes: Scala runs on the JVM, so the classic form is the Java one with Scala syntax: a @volatile flag is the latch (visibility, not just atomicity), shutdown() sets it idempotently, interrupt() or a sentinel wakes the loop, and join()/CountDownLatch.await() is phase 2. An equally common binding is to delegate to java.util.concurrent - an ExecutorService's shutdown plus awaitTermination - which is why this file is classified as library rather than manual. The classic structure is still justified for the single participant that owns resources no executor will release.
pitfalls: @volatile publishes the flag but does not wake a blocked worker: a thread parked in wait/sleep/IO needs interrupt() or a timeout, otherwise phase 2 starts only when that call returns.
Blocking on Await or CountDownLatch inside a JVM/pool thread can starve the executor the worker itself runs on; wait from outside or on a separate ExecutionContext.

f.cancel on a scala.concurrent.Future cannot stop running work in general (the future must be completed and the executor must support interruption); treating it as a stop button skips the second phase entirely.

variants.name: Akka/Pekko ActorSystem.terminate + whenTerminated
variants.implementation_notes: The actor runtime implements the pattern for whole subsystems: terminate() starts CoordinatedShutdown, which walks ordered phases (service-unbind, service-requests-done, service-stop, cluster shutdown, actor system terminate) and returns when the last phase completes - whenTerminated exposes completion as a Future[Terminated], with per-phase timeouts as the forced fallback. Actors receive Stop messages in order and run postStop for their cleanup. Use this variant when the participant is an actor system or cluster member; the flag/join variant covers plain threads and futures inside the same JVM.
variants.code_sketch:
val system = ActorSystem("app")
// ...
system.terminate()                                  // phase 1: CoordinatedShutdown
Await.result(system.whenTerminated, 30.seconds)     // phase 2: Future[Terminated]

// register application cleanup in an ordered phase instead of a shutdown hook
CoordinatedShutdown(system).addTask(
  CoordinatedShutdown.PhaseServiceRequestsDone, "drain")(() => drainAndFlush())
pitfalls: Do not schedule follow-up work (onComplete/onTerminated callbacks) on the terminating system's own dispatcher: it is shut down before the future completes, so the continuation never runs.

Tasks registered in a phase after the shutdown has started are silently ignored; register them early, and remember that phases time out (the next phase starts anyway) unless recover=off is configured.
Awaiting whenTerminated indefinitely hides a stuck phase: the configured phase timeouts are the fallback, and the application should log which phase exceeded its budget.
